steps.text: After Valentinian III murdered Aetius in 454 and was killed himself in 455, Gaiseric sailed from Carthage and plundered Rome for two weeks, carrying off the empress and her daughters. The Vandals seized Sardinia, Corsica, the Balearics and western Sicily and raided the Italian coasts every year. In 468 the two empires sent a huge joint armada under Basiliscus against Carthage, but Gaiseric burned it with fire ships off Cape Bon, ending the last real hope of saving the West.

events.name: Vandal sack of Rome
events.text: Gaiseric's Vandals plundered Rome for fourteen days.

events.name: Battle of Cape Bon
events.text: Vandal fire ships destroyed the joint Roman expedition against Carthage.

steps.label: 472 to 476
steps.title: The last emperor
steps.text: By the 470s the Western emperor ruled little more than Italy: Visigoths held most of Gaul and Spain, Burgundians the Rhone valley, Franks the north and Vandals Africa, and real power lay with barbarian generals. In 476 Odoacer, a Germanic officer, led the army in Italy in mutiny, killed the general Orestes and deposed his young son, the emperor Romulus Augustulus, at Ravenna. Odoacer sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople and ruled as king of Italy, while the Eastern Roman Empire would last almost another thousand years.

moves.label: Mutiny of the army in Italy

events.name: Deposition of Romulus Augustulus
events.text: Odoacer deposed the boy emperor, the conventional end of the Western Roman Empire.

name: Huna invasions of India
summary: The Alchon Huns, steppe invaders known in India as Hunas, crossed the Hindu Kush and attacked the Gupta Empire, which threw them back under Skandagupta about 460. Around 500 their kings Toramana and Mihirakula overran Gandhara, Punjab and central India as far as Malwa, until Indian rulers led by Yashodharman of Mandasor defeated Mihirakula about 528. The Huns were pushed back to Kashmir, but the wars shattered the Gupta Empire and India's classical age ended in a patchwork of regional kingdoms.

steps.label: c. 455 to 467
steps.title: Skandagupta holds the line
steps.text: Having taken Bactria and Kabul, the Alchon Huns under kings such as Khingila pushed through the passes into Gandhara and threatened the Gupta Empire, then at its height across northern India. Emperor Skandagupta led the Gupta army west and drove them back. His pillar inscription at Bhitari boasts that the earth shook when he met the Hunas in battle, and for a generation the Huns stayed beyond the Indus.

moves.label: Alchon Huns cross the Hindu Kush

events.name: Bhitari pillar inscription
events.text: Skandagupta's inscription at Bhitari records his victory over the Hunas.

steps.label: c. 484 to 510
steps.title: Toramana conquers the northwest
steps.text: After Skandagupta's death about 467 the Gupta Empire weakened through succession quarrels. Around 500 the Hun king Toramana led his horsemen out of Gandhara, overran Punjab and Rajasthan and reached Malwa in central India, where an inscription on a great stone boar at Eran is dated to his reign. In 510 the Gupta prince Bhanugupta fought a battle at Eran in which his general Goparaja was killed, and Gupta rule shrank toward the Ganges valley and Bengal.

fronts.label: Approximate limit of Hun rule, c. 510

events.name: Battle of Eran
events.text: A Gupta inscription at Eran records the battle in which Bhanugupta's general Goparaja fell; most historians link it to the Hun advance.

steps.label: c. 515 to 527
steps.title: Mihirakula's empire
steps.text: Toramana's son Mihirakula ruled from Sakala, modern Sialkot, over lands stretching from Gandhara and Kashmir to Gwalior, where an inscription is dated to his fifteenth regnal year. Buddhist sources remember him as a cruel persecutor who burned monasteries in Gandhara. The Chinese pilgrim Song Yun visited the Hun court in Gandhara about 520, when kindred Huns also ruled much of Central Asia.

fronts.label: Approximate limit of Hun rule, c. 520

events.name: Gwalior inscription of Mihirakula
events.text: An inscription at Gwalior fort dated in Mihirakula's reign shows Hun rule deep in central India.

steps.label: c. 528
steps.title: Yashodharman defeats Mihirakula
steps.text: Indian rulers finally combined against the Huns. Yashodharman, king of Mandasor in Malwa, defeated Mihirakula about 528 and set up victory pillars at Sondani claiming that the Hun king had bowed at his feet, while the pilgrim Xuanzang later credited the Gupta king Narasimhagupta Baladitya with capturing and releasing him. Mihirakula withdrew to Kashmir and Hun power in India was broken, but so was the Gupta Empire, which broke up into regional kingdoms within a few decades.

events.name: Battle of Sondani
events.text: Yashodharman's victory pillars at Sondani near Mandasor commemorate his defeat of Mihirakula.

name: Justinian's reconquests
summary: Emperor Justinian I set out to restore Roman rule in the West. His general Belisarius destroyed the Vandal kingdom in Africa in a single campaign in 533 to 534, but the war against the Ostrogoths in Italy dragged on for almost twenty years, through plague and a Gothic revival under Totila, until the eunuch general Narses won in 552 to 554. Africa, Italy and a strip of southern Spain returned to the empire, but Italy was left ruined and the empire overstretched, and the Lombards took much of Italy from 568.

steps.label: 533 to 534
steps.title: The Vandal War
steps.text: Using a Vandal succession dispute as a pretext, Justinian sent Belisarius with about 15,000 men in a fleet of 500 transports. They landed at Caput Vada in September 533 and marched up the coast, and when King Gelimer tried to trap them at Ad Decimum his divided army was routed and Carthage fell the next day. A second defeat at Tricamarum in December broke the Vandals, and Gelimer surrendered in March 534 and was paraded in triumph in Constantinople.

events.name: Battle of Ad Decimum
events.text: Belisarius routed Gelimer's divided army ten Roman miles from Carthage.

events.name: Battle of Tricamarum
events.text: The second defeat ended Vandal resistance; Gelimer fled and surrendered the next spring.

steps.label: 535 to 540
steps.title: Belisarius in Italy
steps.text: The murder of the pro-Roman Gothic queen Amalasuntha gave Justinian his reason to attack the Ostrogoths. In 535 Mundus took Dalmatia and Belisarius took Sicily almost without a fight, then crossed to Italy, stormed Naples and entered Rome in December 536. The new Gothic king Witiges besieged him there for a year from 537 but failed, and as Roman forces pushed north Belisarius closed in on Ravenna, which surrendered in 540 with Witiges inside.

fronts.label: Approximate front during the siege of Rome, 537

events.name: Siege of Rome
events.text: Belisarius held Rome against Witiges for a year until the Goths gave up.

events.name: Surrender of Ravenna
events.text: Witiges handed over the Gothic capital, apparently believing Belisarius would accept the western crown.

steps.label: 541 to 549
steps.title: Totila's revival
steps.text: Belisarius was recalled to face Persia, and in 541 the Goths chose the able Totila as king just as the Plague of Justinian began killing a large share of the empire's people. Totila routed the Roman commanders at Faenza in 542, took Naples in 543 and starved Rome into surrender in December 546. Belisarius came back with too few men and was recalled again in 549, leaving the Goths in control of most of Italy.

events.name: Battle of Faventia
events.text: Totila's small army routed a much larger Roman force near Faenza.

events.name: Totila takes Rome
events.text: Totila took the starving city after a long blockade.

steps.label: 551 to 554
steps.title: Narses ends the Gothic War
steps.text: Justinian finally gave the elderly eunuch Narses a large, well-paid army with Lombard and Herul allies, which marched around the head of the Adriatic to Ravenna in 552 and then down the Via Flaminia. At Taginae his archers and dismounted cavalry crushed the Goths and killed Totila, and the last Gothic king, Teias, fell at Mons Lactarius near Vesuvius that October. In 554 Narses destroyed a Frankish and Alamannic invasion on the Volturnus, and Italy was Roman again, but devastated.

events.name: Battle of Taginae
events.text: Narses' victory killed Totila and broke the Gothic army.

events.name: Battle of Mons Lactarius
events.text: Teias, the last Ostrogothic king, died in a two-day last stand.

events.name: Battle of the Volturnus
events.text: Narses annihilated a Frankish and Alamannic army near Casilinum.

name: Roman-Persian War of 602 to 628
summary: When the usurper Phocas murdered Emperor Maurice in 602, the Sasanian shah Khosrow II invaded to avenge his former patron and began the last and greatest war between Rome and Persia. Persian armies took Mesopotamia, Syria, Jerusalem and Egypt and in 626 besieged Constantinople together with the Avars, but Emperor Heraclius struck deep into Persia, won at Nineveh in 627 and forced a peace that restored the old frontier. The war exhausted both empires only a few years before the Arab conquests overwhelmed them.

steps.label: 602 to 610
steps.title: Khosrow avenges Maurice
steps.text: Khosrow II owed his throne to Emperor Maurice, so when the centurion Phocas killed Maurice and seized power in 602, the shah declared war. The Persians took the great frontier fortress of Dara in 604 and then overran Roman Mesopotamia and Armenia while Phocas purged his own generals. In 610 Heraclius, son of the governor of Africa, sailed from Carthage, overthrew Phocas and became emperor, but inherited a collapsing eastern front.

events.name: Siege of Dara
events.text: After a nine-month siege the Persians took Dara, the key Roman fortress in Mesopotamia.

events.name: Fall of Phocas
events.text: Heraclius's fleet reached Constantinople, Phocas was executed and Heraclius crowned.

steps.label: 611 to 619
steps.title: Persia conquers the East
steps.text: Heraclius's counterattack was beaten outside Antioch in 613, cutting the empire in two. Shahrbaraz took Damascus and in 614 Jerusalem, where thousands died and the True Cross was carried off to Ctesiphon, while Shahin's army reached Chalcedon across the Bosporus from Constantinople. From 618 Shahrbaraz invaded Egypt, and the fall of Alexandria in 619 cost the empire its richest province and the grain that fed the capital.

events.name: Battle of Antioch
events.text: Heraclius's defeat outside Antioch let the Persians split the empire.

events.name: Fall of Jerusalem
events.text: The Persians stormed Jerusalem after a three-week siege and took the True Cross.

events.name: Fall of Alexandria
events.text: Alexandria's fall gave Persia Egypt and its grain.

steps.label: 622 to 625
steps.title: Heraclius strikes back
steps.text: Heraclius bought a truce from the Avars, melted down church treasure to pay his troops and in 622 crossed to Asia Minor, where he trained a new army and beat Shahrbaraz. In 624 he marched through Armenia into Atropatene, the Persian heartland, and destroyed the great fire temple at Ganzak. Wintering in the Caucasus, he outmanoeuvred three Persian armies and in 625 defeated Shahrbaraz again at the bridge over the Sarus in Cilicia.

moves.label: Through the Caucasus to the Sarus, 625

events.name: Sack of Ganzak
events.text: Heraclius destroyed the fire temple of Adur Gushnasp, one of Zoroastrianism's holiest sites, in revenge for Jerusalem.

events.name: Battle of the Sarus
events.text: Heraclius beat Shahrbaraz at the bridge over the Sarus near modern Adana.

steps.title: Siege of Constantinople
steps.text: Khosrow staked everything on a combined strike at the capital: Shahrbaraz camped at Chalcedon on the Asian shore while the Avar khagan brought perhaps 80,000 Avars and Slavs to the land walls. Heraclius stayed in the east, sending part of his army back while his brother Theodore crushed Shahin's army, and went to Lazica to seal an alliance with the Western Turks. In August the defenders, led by the patrician Bonus and Patriarch Sergius, sank the Slav canoes trying to ferry Persians across the Bosporus, and the Avars withdrew.

moves.label: To Lazica to meet the Turks

events.name: Siege of Constantinople
events.text: The Theodosian Walls and the Roman fleet held, and the Avar khagan withdrew in August.

steps.label: 627 to 628
steps.title: Nineveh and peace
steps.text: With the Western Turks storming into the Caucasus and besieging Tiflis alongside him, Heraclius invaded Mesopotamia in autumn 627 and destroyed the army of Rhahzadh near the ruins of Nineveh in December. He sacked Khosrow's palace at Dastagird and approached Ctesiphon. Khosrow was overthrown and killed by his son Kavad II in February 628, and the new shah made peace, giving back all conquered lands and, in 630, the True Cross.

events.name: Battle of Nineveh
events.text: Heraclius killed Rhahzadh and destroyed the last Persian field army.

events.name: Peace of 628
events.text: Kavad II returned all Roman territory, ending the war on the old frontier.

name: Early Muslim conquests
summary: After the death of Muhammad, the Rashidun and then Umayyad caliphs led Arab armies out of Arabia against the exhausted Byzantine and Sasanian empires. Within a century the Caliphate stretched from Spain and Morocco to Central Asia and the Indus, though it failed to take Constantinople and was halted in Gaul and by the Berber Revolt. The conquests spread Islam and Arabic across a vast region and reshaped the medieval world.

steps.label: 632 to 636
steps.title: Yarmouk and Qadisiyyah
steps.text: After Muhammad's death in 632, Caliph Abu Bakr crushed the Ridda revolts and united Arabia, then sent armies against the Byzantine and Sasanian empires, both drained by their recent war. Khalid ibn al-Walid made a famous desert march from Iraq to Syria, Damascus fell in 634 to 635, and in 636 Arab armies won decisively at the Yarmouk against Heraclius's army and at al-Qadisiyyah against the Persian general Rostam.

events.name: Battle of the Yarmouk
events.text: A six-day battle that destroyed the Byzantine field army and cost the empire Syria.

events.name: Battle of al-Qadisiyyah
events.text: The Arab victory over Rostam opened Iraq to conquest.

steps.label: 639 to 642
steps.title: Egypt
steps.text: Amr ibn al-As led a small army from Palestine across Sinai into Egypt at the end of 639. After victory at Heliopolis in 640 and a long siege of the fortress of Babylon, the Byzantines agreed in November 641 to evacuate Alexandria. Egypt gave the Caliphate its grain, its shipyards and a base for the advance west.

events.name: Battle of Heliopolis
events.text: Amr defeated the Byzantine army of Egypt, opening the way to Babylon and Alexandria.

events.name: Treaty of Alexandria
events.text: The patriarch Cyrus agreed to hand over Alexandria, which the Arabs entered in 642.

steps.label: 637 to 651
steps.title: Fall of Persia
steps.text: The Arabs took the Sasanian capital Ctesiphon in 637 and founded garrison cities at Basra and Kufa. Under Caliph Umar they pushed onto the Iranian plateau, and the victory at Nahavand in 642, the Victory of Victories, ended organised Persian resistance. The last shah, Yazdegerd III, fled from province to province until he was killed near Merv in 651, and the Sasanian Empire was gone.

events.name: Fall of Ctesiphon
events.text: The Arabs took the Sasanian capital and its vast treasury.

events.name: Battle of Nahavand
events.text: The Victory of Victories destroyed the last great Sasanian army.

events.name: Death of Yazdegerd III
events.text: The last Sasanian shah was killed near Merv, ending the dynasty.

steps.label: 647 to 709
steps.title: North Africa
steps.text: Raids into Byzantine Africa began in 647, and in 670 Uqba ibn Nafi founded Kairouan as a permanent base. Uqba rode to the Atlantic in 681, but on his return the Berber chief Kusaila ambushed and killed him near Biskra, and Berber resistance under Kusaila and later the queen Kahina held up the conquest for twenty years. Hassan ibn al-Numan took Carthage, Byzantium's last stronghold, in 698, and by about 709 Musa ibn Nusayr had reached the Atlantic coast of Morocco.

moves.label: Kairouan and the ride to the Atlantic

events.name: Founding of Kairouan
events.text: Uqba ibn Nafi founded a garrison city that became the capital of Arab Africa.

events.name: Battle of Vescera
events.text: Kusaila's Berbers and Byzantine allies killed Uqba ibn Nafi near Biskra.

events.name: Fall of Carthage
events.text: Hassan ibn al-Numan took Byzantium's last major stronghold in Africa.

steps.label: 711 to 713
steps.title: Spain, Sindh and Transoxiana
steps.text: In 711 Tariq ibn Ziyad, a Berber commander serving Musa ibn Nusayr, crossed the strait that now bears his name, Gibraltar, and killed the Visigothic king Roderic at the Guadalete; within a few years the Visigothic kingdom had collapsed except in the northern mountains. In the same years Muhammad ibn Qasim conquered Sindh and Qutayba ibn Muslim took Bukhara and Samarkand, carrying the Caliphate to the Indus and the Jaxartes.

events.name: Battle of Guadalete
events.text: Tariq's army destroyed the Visigothic host and King Roderic was killed.

events.name: Fall of Debal
events.text: Muhammad ibn Qasim stormed the port of Debal at the mouth of the Indus and went on to conquer Sindh.

events.name: Capture of Samarkand
events.text: Qutayba ibn Muslim forced Samarkand to submit, completing the conquest of Transoxiana's heartland.

steps.label: 717 to 718
steps.title: Siege of Constantinople
steps.text: The Umayyads made their greatest effort against the Byzantine capital, sending a huge army under Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik and a large fleet. Emperor Leo III held the walls, Greek fire burned the Arab ships, and a harsh winter, Bulgar attacks and hunger forced a disastrous retreat in August 718. The failure kept the Caliphate out of southeastern Europe for centuries.

events.name: Siege of Constantinople
events.text: The failed siege saved Byzantium and blocked a Muslim advance into southeastern Europe.

steps.label: 720 to 732
steps.title: Tours
steps.text: From Spain the Umayyads took Narbonne and raided deep into Gaul, while in the Asturian mountains the Visigothic noble Pelagius won a small victory at Covadonga in 722. In 732 the governor of al-Andalus, Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, crossed the Pyrenees, crushed Duke Odo of Aquitaine and sacked Bordeaux, then headed for the rich abbey of Tours. Charles Martel and the Franks stopped him between Poitiers and Tours, and he was killed in the battle.

events.name: Battle of the River Garonne
events.text: Abd al-Rahman routed Duke Odo of Aquitaine and sacked Bordeaux.

events.name: Battle of Tours
events.text: The Frankish infantry held firm and the Umayyad commander was killed, ending the raid.

steps.label: 739 to 750
steps.title: Limits of expansion
steps.text: The age of rapid conquest ended in a run of setbacks. In 740 Leo III destroyed an Umayyad army at Akroinon, and the same year the Berbers of the Maghreb, angered by heavy taxes and enslavement despite their conversion, rose in a great revolt that drove Arab rule out of Morocco and western Algeria. Overstretched and divided, the Umayyad dynasty was overthrown by the Abbasid revolution, whose armies from Khorasan won at the Zab in 750, and the Caliphate turned from expansion to consolidation.

events.name: Battle of Akroinon
events.text: Leo III destroyed a major Umayyad raiding army in western Anatolia.

events.name: Berber Revolt
events.text: A revolt beginning at Tangier destroyed Arab armies and ended Umayyad rule in the far Maghreb.

events.name: Battle of the Zab
events.text: The Abbasids defeated the last Umayyad caliph, Marwan II, and replaced his dynasty.

name: Reconquista
summary: For nearly eight centuries the Christian kingdoms of northern Iberia fought and bargained with the Muslim states of al-Andalus, pushing the frontier south from the Cantabrian mountains to the Duero, the Tagus, the Guadalquivir and finally Granada. The fall of Granada in 1492 completed the conquest and made Castile and Aragon, soon to be Spain, a crusading Catholic power on the eve of its overseas empire.

steps.title: Covadonga
steps.text: After the Umayyads overran Visigothic Spain in 711, Christian holdouts gathered in the Asturian mountains under the noble Pelagius. Around 722 he ambushed a Muslim column in the valley of Covadonga, and the small Kingdom of Asturias survived behind the Cantabrian range. Later chroniclers made this skirmish the starting point of the Reconquista.

events.name: Battle of Covadonga
events.text: Pelagius's mountaineers routed an Umayyad force, securing an independent Christian kingdom in Asturias.

steps.label: 910 to 1002
steps.title: The Duero frontier and Almanzor
steps.text: Asturias pushed its frontier south to the Duero and moved its capital to León in 910. Abd al-Rahman III proclaimed a caliphate in Córdoba but was beaten by Ramiro II at Simancas in 939. At the end of the century the chamberlain Almanzor struck back with yearly raids, sacking Barcelona in 985 and Santiago de Compostela in 997.

events.name: Battle of Simancas
events.text: Ramiro II of León defeated Caliph Abd al-Rahman III, holding the Duero line.

events.name: Sack of Santiago
events.text: Almanzor burned the shrine city of Santiago, the height of Córdoba's power.

steps.label: 1031 to 1086
steps.title: Taifas, Toledo and the Almoravids
steps.text: The caliphate of Córdoba collapsed in 1031 into rival taifa kingdoms that paid tribute to Christian kings. Alfonso VI of León and Castile took the old Visigothic capital of Toledo in 1085, carrying the frontier to the Tagus. Alarmed, the taifa kings called in the Almoravids of Morocco, whose emir Yusuf ibn Tashfin crushed Alfonso at Sagrajas in 1086.

events.name: Fall of Toledo
events.text: Alfonso VI took Toledo, the first great Muslim city to fall for good.

events.name: Battle of Sagrajas
events.text: Yusuf ibn Tashfin routed Alfonso VI and brought al-Andalus under Almoravid rule.

steps.label: 1086 to 1147
steps.title: Zaragoza and Lisbon
steps.text: The Almoravids reunited al-Andalus and retook Valencia after El Cid's death, but could not regain Toledo. In the Ebro valley Alfonso I of Aragon, the Battler, captured Zaragoza in 1118. In the west Afonso Henriques made Portugal a kingdom and in 1147, helped by crusaders sailing to the Holy Land, took Lisbon.

events.name: Siege of Zaragoza
events.text: Alfonso the Battler took Zaragoza, opening the Ebro valley to Aragon.

events.name: Siege of Lisbon
events.text: Portuguese and northern crusaders captured Lisbon, the future capital of Portugal.

steps.label: 1195 to 1212
steps.title: Las Navas de Tolosa
steps.text: The Almohads, a new Moroccan dynasty, replaced the Almoravids and crushed Alfonso VIII of Castile at Alarcos in 1195. The pope proclaimed a crusade, and in 1212 Alfonso VIII, Peter II of Aragon and Sancho VII of Navarre crossed the Sierra Morena through a hidden pass. They destroyed the army of Caliph Muhammad al-Nasir at Las Navas de Tolosa, breaking Almohad power in Spain.

events.name: Battle of Alarcos
events.text: The Almohads routed Alfonso VIII and pushed the frontier back toward Toledo.

events.name: Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa
events.text: The allied Christian kings shattered the Almohad army, the turning point of the Reconquista.

steps.label: 1228 to 1249
steps.title: Córdoba and Seville
steps.text: As the Almohad state fell apart, Ferdinand III, who united Castile and León in 1230, took Córdoba in 1236 and Seville in 1248. James I of Aragon conquered Majorca in 1229 and Valencia in 1238, and Portugal reached the Algarve in 1249. Only the Nasrid emirate of Granada survived, as a tribute-paying vassal of Castile.

events.name: Fall of Córdoba
events.text: Ferdinand III took the old caliphal capital and turned its great mosque into a cathedral.

events.name: Fall of Valencia
events.text: James I of Aragon captured Valencia after a long siege.

events.name: Fall of Seville
events.text: Seville surrendered to Ferdinand III after a sixteen-month siege by land and river.

steps.label: 1275 to 1350
steps.title: The Battle of the Strait
steps.text: For a century the Marinid sultans of Morocco crossed the Strait of Gibraltar to help Granada. In 1340 Alfonso XI of Castile and Afonso IV of Portugal routed the Marinid sultan Abu al-Hasan and Yusuf I of Granada on the Río Salado near Tarifa. The capture of Algeciras in 1344 closed the strait to further African armies.

events.name: Battle of Río Salado
events.text: Castile and Portugal crushed the last great Moroccan army to invade Iberia.

events.name: Siege of Algeciras
events.text: Alfonso XI took the key port on the strait after a two-year siege.

steps.label: 1482 to 1492
steps.title: The Fall of Granada
steps.text: Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon, married in 1469, launched the final war on Granada in 1482. Exploiting a civil war between Muhammad XII, known as Boabdil, and his uncle al-Zagal, they took Málaga in 1487 and Baza in 1489, then besieged Granada from their camp city of Santa Fe. Boabdil surrendered the Alhambra on 2 January 1492, ending Muslim rule in Iberia.

events.name: Siege of Málaga
events.text: The fall of Málaga cut Granada off from help by sea.

events.name: Surrender of Granada
events.text: Boabdil handed over the Alhambra to Isabella and Ferdinand, completing the Reconquista.

name: Battle of Talas and the An Lushan Rebellion
summary: In 751 an Abbasid army, helped by the defection of Karluk Turks, defeated the Tang general Gao Xianzhi near the Talas river, marking the western limit of Chinese power in Central Asia. Four years later the Tang frontier general An Lushan rebelled, took both Chinese capitals and proclaimed his own Yan dynasty. The Tang recovered only with the help of Uyghur cavalry and by 763 the rebellion was over, but China had suffered enormous loss of life, withdrawn its western garrisons and lost much central control to regional governors.

steps.title: Talas
steps.text: Tang China had extended its Anxi protectorate across the Tarim basin and over the Tian Shan, while the new Abbasid Caliphate was consolidating Transoxiana. When the Korean-born Tang general Gao Xianzhi overthrew the ruler of Tashkent, the city's allies appealed to the Arabs, and Gao marched west with Tang troops and Karluk and Ferghana auxiliaries. Near the Talas river in July 751 the Karluks changed sides in the middle of a five-day battle, and the Tang army was destroyed by the Abbasid general Ziyad ibn Salih.

events.name: Battle of Talas
events.text: The defection of the Karluks turned the battle, and Gao Xianzhi escaped with only a few thousand men.

steps.label: 755 to 756
steps.title: An Lushan takes the capitals
steps.text: An Lushan, a general of Sogdian and Turkic descent who commanded three frontier armies in the northeast, rebelled in December 755 against the chief minister Yang Guozhong. His veteran troops swept down the North China Plain, took Luoyang within weeks and in 756 broke through the Tong Pass, where Geshu Han's army was destroyed. Emperor Xuanzong fled toward Sichuan, his soldiers forced him to have his consort Yang Guifei killed at Mawei, and the crown prince proclaimed himself emperor Suzong at Lingwu.

events.name: Fall of Luoyang
events.text: An Lushan took the eastern capital and proclaimed himself emperor of Yan.

events.name: Battle of Tong Pass
events.text: Forced by the court to attack, Geshu Han's army was destroyed and the road to Chang'an lay open.

events.name: Mawei incident
events.text: Mutinous guards killed Yang Guozhong and forced the emperor to have Yang Guifei put to death.

steps.title: Recapture with Uyghur help
steps.text: An Lushan, half blind and violent, was murdered by his son An Qingxu in January 757. At Suiyang the Tang commander Zhang Xun held out for most of the year against a huge besieging army, shielding the rich Huai and Yangtze lands that fed the Tang war effort. In the autumn Guo Ziyi and the prince Li Chu, reinforced by Uyghur cavalry sent by the Uyghur khagan, won at Xiangji Temple, retook Chang'an and then Luoyang.

fronts.label: Rebel line on the Yellow River, late 757

events.name: Siege of Suiyang
events.text: Zhang Xun's garrison held for ten months before falling, but by then the south was safe.

events.name: Battle of Xiangji Temple
events.text: Tang and Uyghur troops won a hard battle south of Chang'an, and the capital was retaken days later.

events.name: Recapture of Luoyang
events.text: The rebels abandoned the eastern capital and fell back across the Yellow River.

steps.label: 758 to 763
steps.title: Shi Siming and the end of the rebellion
steps.text: A Tang siege of An Qingxu at Yecheng collapsed in 759 when a sandstorm scattered the besiegers and the rebel general Shi Siming arrived, killed An Qingxu, took over the rebellion and retook Luoyang. Shi Siming was in turn murdered by his son Shi Chaoyi in 761, and in 762 Tang and Uyghur forces recovered Luoyang for good. In early 763 Shi Chaoyi, deserted by his generals, killed himself, but the rebel commanders were pardoned as semi-independent governors and the Tang never regained their old strength.

events.name: Battle of Yecheng
events.text: Nine Tang armies without a supreme commander were scattered, giving the rebellion a second life.

events.name: Tang retake Luoyang
events.text: Tang and Uyghur troops recovered the eastern capital, which the Uyghurs then plundered.

events.name: End of the rebellion
events.text: Abandoned by his generals, Shi Chaoyi killed himself near Fanyang.

name: Charlemagne's wars
summary: Charlemagne, king of the Franks from 768, campaigned almost every year of his reign. He conquered the Lombard kingdom of Italy in 774, subdued and forcibly converted the pagan Saxons in thirty years of brutal fighting, carved out a Spanish March south of the Pyrenees and destroyed the Avar khaganate in the 790s. Crowned emperor in Rome in 800, he ruled the largest state in the West since Rome, the core of later France, Germany and Italy.

sides.name: Saxons, Lombards, Moors, Avars and Danes

steps.title: War on the Saxons
steps.text: The Saxons between the Rhine and the Elbe were pagan, independent and constantly raiding the Frankish border. In 772 Charlemagne marched from Worms, stormed the Saxon stronghold of Eresburg and cut down the Irminsul, their sacred pillar, opening a war that would last more than thirty years.

events.name: Destruction of the Irminsul
events.text: Charlemagne took Eresburg and destroyed the Saxons' holiest shrine.

steps.label: 773 to 774
steps.title: Conquest of the Lombards
steps.text: When the Lombard king Desiderius threatened Rome, Pope Adrian I called on Charlemagne. In 773 the Franks crossed the Alps in two columns, Charlemagne by the Mont Cenis and his uncle Bernard by the Great St Bernard, turned the Lombard defences at the Alpine passes and shut Desiderius up in Pavia. Pavia surrendered in June 774 after a nine-month siege, and Charlemagne made himself King of the Lombards.

events.name: Siege of Pavia
events.text: The Lombard capital surrendered and Desiderius ended his life in a Frankish monastery.

steps.title: Roncevaux and the Spanish March
steps.text: Invited by Muslim governors rebelling against the emir of Cordoba, Abd al-Rahman I, Charlemagne led two armies into Spain in 778, but Zaragoza shut its gates and news of a Saxon revolt called him home. As the army recrossed the Pyrenees, Basques ambushed the rearguard at Roncevaux Pass and killed its commanders, among them Roland, later the hero of the Song of Roland. The Franks returned more cautiously, taking Girona in 785.

events.name: Battle of Roncevaux Pass
events.text: Basque fighters destroyed the Frankish rearguard, killing Roland, prefect of the Breton March.

steps.label: 777 to 785
steps.title: Widukind and Verden
steps.text: Charlemagne held an assembly at Paderborn in the heart of Saxony in 777, but the Saxon noble Widukind repeatedly roused the country against Frankish rule and forced baptism. After the Saxons destroyed a Frankish army in the Suntel hills in 782, Charlemagne had some 4,500 Saxon prisoners beheaded at Verden. Campaigning even through the winters that followed, he wore down resistance until Widukind surrendered and was baptized in 785.

events.name: Battle of the Suntel
events.text: The Saxons wiped out a Frankish force in the Suntel hills.

events.name: Massacre of Verden
events.text: Charlemagne had some 4,500 Saxon captives executed.

events.name: Baptism of Widukind
events.text: The Saxon leader submitted and was baptized at Attigny with Charlemagne as godfather.

steps.label: 788 to 796
steps.title: Destruction of the Avars
steps.text: After deposing his cousin Duke Tassilo of Bavaria in 788, Charlemagne bordered the Avar khaganate, whose horsemen had raided Europe for two centuries. In 791 he led armies down both banks of the Danube as far as the Raab, and in 795 to 796 Duke Eric of Friuli and Charlemagne's son Pepin of Italy stormed the Ring, the Avars' great fortified camp, and carried off its treasure in fifteen wagons. Avar power collapsed and the middle Danube was opened to Frankish rule and missionaries.

moves.commander: Eric of Friuli and Pepin of Italy
moves.label: Assault on the Ring, 795 to 796

events.name: Fall of the Avar Ring
events.text: The Franks plundered the Avar treasure camp between the Danube and the Tisza; its exact site is unknown.

steps.label: 800 to 811
steps.title: Emperor of the West
steps.text: On Christmas Day 800 Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor of the Romans in St Peter's. His son Louis took Barcelona in 801 to anchor the Spanish March, and in 804 the last Saxons beyond the Elbe were deported and Saxony annexed. A new danger rose in the north, where King Godfred of Denmark fortified the Danevirke and raided Frisia; after Godfred's murder the Treaty of Heiligen in 811 fixed the border on the Eider river.

events.name: Coronation of Charlemagne
events.text: Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor, reviving the imperial title in the West.

events.name: Siege of Barcelona
events.text: Louis the Pious took Barcelona, which became the capital of the Spanish March.

events.name: Treaty of Heiligen
events.text: Franks and Danes agreed on the Eider as their border.

name: Viking invasions
summary: From the raid on Lindisfarne in 793, seafarers from Norway, Denmark and Sweden plundered, traded and settled from Ireland to the Volga. Danish armies conquered much of England until Alfred the Great and his heirs fought them back, a Viking chief received Normandy from the Frankish king in 911, Swedish Rus founded the state of Kyivan Rus, and in the early 1000s Danish kings ruled England itself. The Viking Age is conventionally ended in 1066, when Harald Hardrada died at Stamford Bridge and William of Normandy, a descendant of Vikings, conquered England.

steps.label: 793 to 800
steps.title: Lindisfarne
steps.text: In June 793 raiders from Norway sacked the monastery of Lindisfarne off the Northumbrian coast, killing monks and carrying off treasure and captives, and the scholar Alcuin wrote that such terror had never before been seen in Britain. Iona and other undefended island monasteries in Scotland and Ireland were struck within a few years. Fast, shallow-draught longships let small crews strike almost anywhere on the coasts and rivers of Europe and be gone before defenders could gather.

events.name: Raid on Lindisfarne
events.text: The sack of Lindisfarne is traditionally taken as the start of the Viking Age.

events.name: Raid on Iona
events.text: Raiders struck the monastery of St Columba, the first of several attacks.

steps.label: 834 to 845
steps.title: Raids become invasions
steps.text: From the 830s the raids grew into campaigns by fleets of a hundred ships or more, exploiting the civil wars among Charlemagne's grandsons. Norsemen founded Dublin in 841 as a fortified base, a fleet sacked Seville in 844 before being beaten at Tablada, and in 845 a Danish chieftain usually identified as Ragnar sailed up the Seine and took Paris, leaving only after Charles the Bald paid 7,000 pounds of silver.

events.name: Founding of Dublin
events.text: Norsemen built a fortified ship base that grew into Ireland's chief town.

events.name: Sack of Seville
events.text: Vikings sacked Seville but were routed at Tablada by the emir's army.

events.name: Siege of Paris
events.text: Ragnar's fleet took Paris and left only after a huge payment of silver.

steps.label: 865 to 886
steps.title: The Great Heathen Army
steps.text: In 865 a large Danish army led by Ivar the Boneless and Halfdan landed in East Anglia, bent on conquest rather than plunder. It took York in 866, killed King Edmund of East Anglia and overran Mercia, leaving Wessex under Alfred as the last English kingdom standing. Surprised by Guthrum at Chippenham in January 878, Alfred hid in the Somerset marshes, then raised the levies and crushed the Danes at Edington; Guthrum accepted baptism, and England was divided between Wessex and the Danish-ruled Danelaw.

events.name: Capture of York
events.text: The Danes seized York, which became the capital of a Viking kingdom.

events.name: Battle of Edington
events.text: Alfred's victory saved Wessex and forced Guthrum to make peace.

events.name: Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum
events.text: The treaty fixed the boundary between Wessex and the Danelaw.

steps.label: 860 to 907
steps.title: The Rus in the east
steps.text: Swedish Vikings, called Rus or Varangians, pushed down the rivers of eastern Europe to trade silver, furs and slaves with Byzantium and the Caliphate. A Rus fleet attacked Constantinople in 860, and according to the Russian Primary Chronicle Rurik took power in Novgorod about 862 and his kinsman Oleg seized Kyiv in 882, uniting the route from the Baltic to the Black Sea. Oleg's expedition against Constantinople in 907 won a favourable trade treaty, and his realm grew into Kyivan Rus.

events.name: Rus attack on Constantinople
events.text: A Rus fleet ravaged the suburbs of Constantinople before withdrawing.

events.name: Rurik at Novgorod
events.text: The chronicle says the Novgorodians invited Rurik to rule them.

events.name: Oleg takes Kyiv
events.text: Oleg killed Askold and Dir and made Kyiv his capital.

steps.label: 885 to 911
steps.title: Paris and Normandy
steps.text: In 885 a great Viking army of several hundred ships besieged Paris, which Count Odo held for nearly a year until Emperor Charles the Fat paid the Vikings off and let them ravage Burgundy. Viking bands then settled along the lower Seine under a leader named Rollo. After Rollo was beaten at Chartres in 911, King Charles the Simple granted him the lands around Rouen by the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte in return for baptism and defending the Seine, founding the duchy of Normandy.

events.name: Siege of Paris
events.text: Count Odo's defence held the city through 885 and 886, though the emperor then bought the Vikings off.

events.name: Battle of Chartres
events.text: Frankish forces drove Rollo back from Chartres.

events.name: Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte
events.text: Charles the Simple granted Rollo the lower Seine, the origin of Normandy.

steps.label: 910 to 954
steps.title: England fights back
steps.text: Alfred's son Edward the Elder and his daughter Aethelflaed, Lady of the Mercians, built fortified burhs and reconquered the southern Danelaw after victory at Tettenhall in 910. Alfred's grandson Aethelstan took York in 927 and in 937 crushed an alliance of Olaf Guthfrithson, Norse king of Dublin, with the Scots and Strathclyde Britons at Brunanburh. York changed hands several times more until its last Viking king, Eric Bloodaxe, was driven out and killed in 954, leaving England a single kingdom.

events.name: Battle of Tettenhall
events.text: The Northumbrian Danes were crushed on their way home from a raid.

events.name: Battle of Brunanburh
events.text: Aethelstan defeated the Norse and their Scottish allies; the site is disputed but often placed on the Wirral.

events.name: Death of Eric Bloodaxe
events.text: The last Viking king of York was killed at Stainmore.

steps.label: 980 to 1016
steps.title: The Danish conquest of England
steps.text: Raiding resumed in the 980s against the weak king Aethelred the Unready, who after the defeat at Maldon in 991 paid ever larger sums of Danegeld. In 1013 King Sweyn Forkbeard of Denmark conquered England, and after his death his son Cnut beat Edmund Ironside at Assandun in 1016 and became king of all England, later adding Norway to a North Sea empire. Far to the west, Norse settlers had meanwhile reached Iceland, Greenland and, about 1000, North America.

events.name: Battle of Maldon
events.text: Vikings killed Ealdorman Byrhtnoth, and England began paying Danegeld.

events.name: Battle of Assandun
events.text: Cnut's victory over Edmund Ironside made him king of England.

steps.title: Stamford Bridge and Hastings
steps.text: In September 1066 Harald Hardrada, king of Norway and the most famous Viking warrior of his day, landed in Yorkshire with Tostig, the exiled brother of King Harold Godwinson, and beat the northern earls at Fulford. Harold marched north at speed and destroyed the Norwegian army at Stamford Bridge, killing Hardrada. Three days later Duke William of Normandy, a descendant of Rollo, landed at Pevensey; Harold raced south and was killed at Hastings on 14 October, and the Norman Conquest is often taken as the end of the Viking Age.

events.name: Battle of Fulford
events.text: Hardrada and Tostig beat the earls Edwin and Morcar outside York.

events.name: Battle of Stamford Bridge
events.text: Harold Godwinson destroyed the Norwegian army and Harald Hardrada was killed.

events.name: Battle of Hastings
events.text: William of Normandy defeated and killed Harold, beginning the Norman conquest of England.

name: Struggle for Sicily and southern Italy
summary: Aghlabid armies from Tunisia spent 75 years taking Sicily from the Byzantine Empire, which then kept trying to win it back. In the 11th century Norman mercenaries turned conquerors under Robert Guiscard and Roger I, driving the Byzantines out of southern Italy and taking Sicily from its Muslim emirs by 1091. Their conquests became the Kingdom of Sicily, a meeting point of Latin, Greek and Arab culture.

steps.label: 827 to 831
steps.title: The Aghlabid landing
steps.text: A rebel Byzantine admiral, Euphemius, invited the Aghlabid emirs of Ifriqiya into Sicily. In 827 the aged jurist Asad ibn al-Furat landed at Mazara with about 10,000 men and marched on Syracuse, but plague broke the siege. Reinforcements took Palermo in 831, which became the capital of Muslim Sicily.

events.name: Landing at Mazara
events.text: The Aghlabid army came ashore at Mazara and defeated the local Byzantine forces.

events.name: Fall of Palermo
events.text: Palermo fell after a year-long siege and became the Muslim capital of the island.

steps.label: 831 to 878
steps.title: Enna and Syracuse
steps.text: The conquest went fortress by fortress across the mountainous interior, while Arab raiders also struck mainland Italy and even sacked the outskirts of Rome in 846. Enna, the island's central stronghold, fell in 859. In 878 Syracuse, the Byzantine capital of Sicily, was stormed after a nine-month siege.

events.name: Fall of Enna
events.text: The Aghlabids took the central fortress of Castrogiovanni through a sewer tunnel.

events.name: Fall of Syracuse
events.text: Syracuse was stormed and sacked, leaving the Byzantines only the northeast corner.

steps.label: 902 to 965
steps.title: Taormina and Rometta
steps.text: Emir Ibrahim II took Taormina in 902, the last major Byzantine town. Under the Kalbid emirs, governors for the Fatimids, Sicily became a prosperous Arab island with Palermo one of the largest cities in Europe. A Byzantine expedition in 964 to 965 was crushed and the hill fort of Rometta, the last Christian holdout, fell.

events.name: Fall of Taormina
events.text: Ibrahim II stormed Taormina, the last important Byzantine city on the island.

events.name: Fall of Rometta
events.text: After the Byzantine relief army was destroyed, Rometta surrendered and the conquest was complete.

steps.label: 1038 to 1040
steps.title: Maniakes's counterattack
steps.text: Exploiting a civil war among the Kalbid emirs, the Byzantine general George Maniakes invaded with a mixed army that included Norman mercenaries and the Varangian Harald Hardrada. He took Messina, won at Troina in 1040 and captured Syracuse. He was then recalled to Constantinople under suspicion, and his gains were soon lost, but the Normans had seen how rich and divided Sicily was.

events.name: Battle of Troina
events.text: Maniakes routed the Kalbid army, but Byzantine infighting threw away the victory.

steps.label: 1041 to 1071
steps.title: Robert Guiscard takes the mainland
steps.text: Normans hired to fight in southern Italy turned on their employers, defeating the Byzantines and in 1053 even a papal army at Civitate. Robert Guiscard, made Duke of Apulia and Calabria by the pope in 1059, took Reggio in 1060. When Bari fell to him in 1071 after a three-year siege, five centuries of Byzantine rule in Italy ended.

events.name: Battle of Civitate
events.text: The Normans crushed Pope Leo IX's army and forced the papacy to accept them.

events.name: Fall of Bari
events.text: Robert Guiscard took Bari, the last Byzantine stronghold in Italy.

steps.label: 1061 to 1072
steps.title: Roger crosses to Sicily
steps.text: Invited by one of the quarrelling emirs, Robert's younger brother Roger crossed the Strait and took Messina in 1061. With a few hundred knights he beat a far larger Muslim army at Cerami in 1063. In 1072 the brothers besieged Palermo by land and sea and took the capital.

events.name: Battle of Cerami
events.text: Roger's small Norman force routed a much larger Muslim army.

events.name: Fall of Palermo
events.text: Robert and Roger took the capital after a five-month siege.

steps.label: 1073 to 1091
steps.title: The last emirs
steps.text: Roger, now Count of Sicily, spent two more decades reducing the remaining Muslim strongholds in the south and east. The emir Ibn Abbad of Syracuse was killed in a sea battle in 1086, and Noto, the last town, surrendered in 1091, the same year Roger took Malta. Muslim subjects kept their faith under Norman rule, and their skills helped build the Kingdom of Sicily.

events.name: Fall of Syracuse
events.text: Roger killed Emir Ibn Abbad at sea and took Syracuse.

events.name: Surrender of Noto
events.text: The last Muslim town in Sicily surrendered to Roger I.

name: Byzantine-Bulgarian wars of Basil II
summary: After Byzantium conquered eastern Bulgaria in 971, Tsar Samuel rebuilt the Bulgarian state from Macedonia and raided deep into Greece. Emperor Basil II answered with forty years of campaigning, destroying Samuel's army at Kleidion in 1014 and annexing all of Bulgaria in 1018. The victory earned Basil the name Bulgar-slayer and returned the Danube frontier to Byzantium for the first time in centuries.

steps.label: 976 to 986
steps.title: Samuel's rising and Trajan's Gate
steps.text: When John Tzimiskes died in 976, the four Cometopuli brothers led a revolt in western Bulgaria, and Samuel soon emerged as its ruler. He raided Thessaly and took Larissa in 986. The young Basil II marched to besiege Sredets, modern Sofia, but on his retreat Samuel ambushed and routed him in the pass of Trajan's Gate.

events.name: Fall of Larissa
events.text: Samuel took the Thessalian city and carried off its people and relics.

events.name: Battle of the Gates of Trajan
events.text: Samuel ambushed Basil's retreating army, one of the worst Byzantine defeats of the age.

steps.label: 987 to 997
steps.title: Samuel's high tide and Spercheios
steps.text: While Basil fought rebel generals and eastern wars, Samuel retook northeastern Bulgaria and raided as far as the Peloponnese. In 997 the general Nikephoros Ouranos caught Samuel's returning army camped on the Spercheios river in Greece. A night attack across the flooded river destroyed it, and Samuel and his son barely escaped.

events.name: Battle of Spercheios
events.text: Ouranos destroyed Samuel's army in a surprise attack, ending Bulgarian raids into Greece.

steps.label: 1000 to 1005
steps.title: The yearly campaigns
steps.text: Basil now campaigned every year to grind down Bulgaria. His generals took the old capitals of Pliska and Preslav in 1000, and Basil himself took Vidin on the Danube after an eight-month siege. In 1004 he beat Samuel near Skopje, leaving the Bulgarian heartland in Macedonia surrounded.

events.name: Siege of Vidin
events.text: Basil took the Danube fortress, cutting Samuel off from the north.

events.name: Battle of Skopje
events.text: Basil defeated Samuel on the Vardar and took Skopje.

steps.title: Kleidion
steps.text: Samuel blocked the Kleidion pass below Mount Belasitsa with a long wall. While Basil attacked the front, Nikephoros Xiphias led troops over the mountain and fell on the Bulgarians from behind. Basil reportedly blinded some 15,000 prisoners and sent them home, and Samuel died of a stroke when they reached him at Prilep.

events.name: Battle of Kleidion
events.text: Basil's outflanking attack annihilated Samuel's army.

events.name: Death of Samuel
events.text: Samuel collapsed on seeing his blinded soldiers and died two days later.

steps.label: 1015 to 1018
steps.title: The end of the First Bulgarian Empire
steps.text: Samuel's son Gavril Radomir was murdered by his cousin Ivan Vladislav, who fought on until he was killed besieging Dyrrhachium in 1018. Basil entered Ohrid, the last capital, and the Bulgarian nobles and royal family submitted. Bulgaria became Byzantine provinces for the next 167 years.

events.name: Siege of Dyrrhachium
events.text: Ivan Vladislav was killed attacking the Byzantine port, and Bulgarian resistance collapsed.

events.name: Submission at Ohrid
events.text: The Bulgarian court surrendered to Basil II, ending the First Bulgarian Empire.

name: Seljuk conquests
summary: Oghuz Turkish nomads led by the Seljuk brothers Tughril and Chaghri seized Khorasan from the Ghaznavids, then Persia and Iraq, where Tughril entered Baghdad in 1055 as protector of the Abbasid caliph. Alp Arslan's victory at Manzikert in 1071 opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement, and under Malik Shah the empire stretched from Central Asia to the Mediterranean. Its breakup after 1092 left the divided Muslim Levant that the crusaders would find.

steps.label: 1037 to 1040
steps.title: Dandanaqan
steps.text: The Seljuk clan led its Turkmen herds across the Oxus into Ghaznavid Khorasan, and Tughril was proclaimed ruler in Nishapur in 1038. Sultan Mas'ud of Ghazni brought a heavy army with war elephants to drive them out. Near Merv in 1040 the mobile Turkish horse archers cut it off from water and routed it at Dandanaqan, and the Ghaznavids withdrew east.

events.name: Tughril takes Nishapur
events.text: The capital of Khorasan opened its gates and the khutba was read in Tughril's name.

events.name: Battle of Dandanaqan
events.text: The Seljuks destroyed the Ghaznavid army, winning Khorasan and an empire.

steps.label: 1041 to 1055
steps.title: Persia and Baghdad
steps.text: Tughril swept west across the Iranian plateau, making Rayy his capital and taking Isfahan in 1051. The Buyid emirs who controlled the Abbasid caliph were weak and divided, and in 1055 Tughril entered Baghdad at the caliph's invitation. The caliph named him sultan, and the Seljuks became the champions of Sunni Islam against the Shia Fatimids of Egypt.

events.name: Fall of Isfahan
events.text: Tughril took Isfahan after a year-long siege.

events.name: Tughril enters Baghdad
events.text: The caliph proclaimed Tughril sultan, ending a century of Buyid rule.

steps.label: 1064 to 1071
steps.title: Manzikert
steps.text: Tughril's nephew Alp Arslan took the Armenian capital Ani in 1064, and Turkmen raiders pushed into Byzantine Anatolia. Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes marched east with a huge army while Alp Arslan was campaigning in Syria. Alp Arslan turned north, and at Manzikert in August 1071 the Byzantine army broke and Romanos was captured.

events.name: Fall of Ani
events.text: Alp Arslan stormed the Armenian capital, opening the road west.

events.name: Battle of Manzikert
events.text: Alp Arslan routed and captured Romanos IV, leaving Anatolia open to the Turks.

steps.label: 1072 to 1092
steps.title: Anatolia, Syria and the peak under Malik Shah
steps.text: Byzantium fell into civil war after Manzikert, and Turkmen bands spread across Anatolia. Suleiman ibn Qutalmish made Nicaea, almost in sight of Constantinople, the capital of what became the Sultanate of Rum. In the south the commander Atsiz took Jerusalem in 1073 and Damascus in 1076 from the Fatimids, but when Malik Shah died in 1092 the empire split among his heirs.

events.name: Suleiman takes Nicaea
events.text: Nicaea became the capital of the Seljuks of Rum, close to Constantinople.

events.name: Fall of Jerusalem
events.text: Atsiz took Jerusalem from the Fatimids.

events.name: Death of Malik Shah
events.text: The sultan's death, weeks after his vizier Nizam al-Mulk was murdered, split the empire.

name: Norman Conquest of England
summary: When Edward the Confessor died childless in January 1066, Harold Godwinson took the English crown, but both Harald Hardrada of Norway and William, Duke of Normandy, invaded to claim it. Harold beat the Norwegians at Stamford Bridge and was killed by William at Hastings weeks later, and William crushed English and Danish resistance by 1071. The conquest replaced the Anglo-Saxon elite with a French-speaking Norman aristocracy and tied England to continental Europe.

steps.label: Sep 1066
steps.title: Fulford and Stamford Bridge
steps.text: Harald Hardrada of Norway, joined by Harold's exiled brother Tostig, sailed up the Humber and beat the northern earls at Fulford outside York on 20 September. King Harold, who had spent the summer guarding the south coast, marched north from London in about four days. On 25 September he surprised and destroyed the Norwegians at Stamford Bridge, killing Hardrada and Tostig.

events.name: Battle of Fulford
events.text: Hardrada defeated Earls Edwin and Morcar and York submitted.

events.name: Battle of Stamford Bridge
events.text: Harold destroyed the Norwegian army, ending the Viking age invasions of England.

steps.label: Oct 1066
steps.title: Hastings
steps.text: Two days after Stamford Bridge, the wind turned and William's fleet crossed from Saint-Valery to Pevensey. Harold raced back south and gave battle on 14 October on a ridge near Hastings. After a day of Norman cavalry charges and feigned retreats, Harold was killed and the English shield wall broke.

events.name: Landing at Pevensey
events.text: William's army landed unopposed on 28 September.

events.name: Battle of Hastings
events.text: Harold was killed and the Anglo-Saxon army destroyed.

steps.label: Nov to Dec 1066
steps.title: Encircling London
steps.text: Rather than storm London, William took Dover and Canterbury and then swung west in a wide loop, burning the countryside, and crossed the Thames at Wallingford. At Berkhamsted the English leaders, including the young claimant Edgar Atheling, came out to submit. William was crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066.

events.name: Submission at Berkhamsted
events.text: Edgar Atheling and the English magnates surrendered to William.

events.name: Coronation of William
events.text: William was crowned King of England at Westminster on Christmas Day.

steps.label: 1068 to 1070
steps.title: Northern risings and the Harrying
steps.text: Revolts broke out at Exeter in 1068 and across the north, where Edgar Atheling joined the rebels. In 1069 a Danish fleet sent by Sweyn II sailed into the Humber and, with the English, stormed York and killed its Norman garrison. William bought off the Danes and over the winter laid waste to Yorkshire, a famine campaign remembered as the Harrying of the North.

events.name: Rising at York
events.text: English rebels and Danes stormed York and massacred its Norman garrison.

events.name: Harrying of the North
events.text: William's army burned crops and herds across Yorkshire, killing thousands through famine.

steps.label: 1070 to 1071
steps.title: Hereward and the Isle of Ely
steps.text: In 1070 King Sweyn arrived in person and, with the rebel Hereward, sacked Peterborough Abbey before accepting a payment to leave. The last rebels gathered on the Isle of Ely, an island in the Fens. William built a causeway across the marsh and took Ely in 1071, and Earl Morcar was captured while Hereward escaped into legend.

events.name: Sack of Peterborough
events.text: Hereward and the Danes plundered the abbey to keep its treasure from the Normans.

events.name: Siege of Ely
events.text: The fall of Ely ended organised English resistance.

name: The Crusades
summary: Western European Christians launched a series of armed pilgrimages to win and hold Jerusalem and the Holy Land against the Muslim powers of the Near East. The First Crusade founded the crusader states, but Zengi, Saladin and the Mamluks won them back, the Fourth Crusade turned on Christian Constantinople, and the fall of Acre in 1291 ended the crusader presence. The wars deepened the split between Latin and Greek Christians and widened trade and contact between Europe and the Islamic world.

steps.label: 1096 to 1099
steps.title: First Crusade
steps.text: Answering Pope Urban II's call, armies of French, Norman and Italian knights gathered at Constantinople and crossed into Anatolia, defeating the Seljuk sultan Kilij Arslan at Dorylaeum. After a brutal siege of Antioch they marched down the coast and stormed Jerusalem in July 1099, massacring many of its inhabitants. Four crusader states were founded at Edessa, Antioch, Tripoli and Jerusalem.

fronts.label: Inland edge of the crusader states, c. 1100

events.name: Battle of Dorylaeum
events.text: The crusaders defeated Kilij Arslan's Seljuk army and opened the road across Anatolia.

events.name: Siege of Antioch
events.text: After taking the city by treachery, the crusaders broke out and routed Kerbogha's relief army.

events.name: Siege of Jerusalem
events.text: The crusaders stormed the city and founded the Kingdom of Jerusalem.

steps.label: 1144 to 1149
steps.title: Second Crusade
steps.text: Zengi, atabeg of Mosul and Aleppo, captured Edessa in 1144, destroying the first crusader state. Louis VII of France and Conrad III of Germany led a new crusade, but both armies suffered badly crossing Anatolia. Their joint siege of Damascus collapsed after four days, and Zengi's son Nur ad-Din went on to unite Muslim Syria.

events.name: Fall of Edessa
events.text: Zengi's capture of Edessa triggered the Second Crusade.

events.name: Siege of Damascus
events.text: The crusader siege failed within days and the crusade broke up.

steps.title: Hattin and the fall of Jerusalem
steps.text: Saladin, the Ayyubid sultan, united Egypt and Syria and invaded the Kingdom of Jerusalem. He lured King Guy's army into the waterless hills near Tiberias and destroyed it at the Horns of Hattin. Jerusalem surrendered in October, and within months only Tyre, Tripoli and Antioch were left in crusader hands.

fronts.label: Frontier of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, July 1187

events.name: Battle of Hattin
events.text: Saladin destroyed the crusader field army and captured King Guy.

events.name: Fall of Jerusalem
events.text: Jerusalem surrendered to Saladin after a short siege.

steps.label: 1189 to 1192
steps.title: Third Crusade
steps.text: Frederick Barbarossa led a German army across Anatolia but drowned in the Saleph river. Richard I of England, who seized Cyprus on the way, and Philip II of France arrived by sea and took Acre after a two-year siege, and Richard beat Saladin at Arsuf. Neither side could win outright, and the Treaty of Jaffa left Jerusalem to Saladin and the coast to the crusaders.

events.name: Siege of Acre
events.text: The crusaders captured Acre, which became the new capital of the kingdom.

events.name: Battle of Arsuf
events.text: Richard's disciplined march held off Saladin's attacks and then routed his army.

events.name: Treaty of Jaffa
events.text: A three-year truce left Jerusalem Muslim but open to Christian pilgrims.

steps.label: 1202 to 1204
steps.title: Fourth Crusade
steps.text: Short of money to pay Venice for its fleet, the crusaders led by Boniface of Montferrat and Doge Enrico Dandolo were diverted first to Zara and then to Constantinople to restore a Byzantine claimant. When the deal collapsed they stormed the city in April 1204 and sacked it for three days. They set up a Latin Empire there instead of going on to the Holy Land, a wound that never healed between Catholic and Orthodox Christians.

events.name: Siege of Zara
events.text: The crusaders sacked the Christian city of Zara for Venice and were excommunicated.

events.name: Sack of Constantinople
events.text: Crusaders stormed the Byzantine capital and plundered it for three days.

steps.label: 1217 to 1250
steps.title: Crusades against Egypt
steps.text: Seeing Egypt as the key to Jerusalem, the Fifth Crusade took Damietta in 1219 but was trapped by the Nile flood. Emperor Frederick II regained Jerusalem by treaty in 1229, but it was lost for good in 1244. Louis IX of France took Damietta again in 1249 and advanced on Cairo, but his army was destroyed at Mansurah and he was captured, and in the turmoil the Mamluks seized power in Egypt.

events.name: Siege of Damietta
events.text: The Fifth Crusade took the Nile port after an eighteen-month siege.

events.name: Battle of Mansurah
events.text: Ayyubid and Mamluk troops destroyed the crusader army, leading to Louis IX's capture.

steps.label: 1260 to 1291
steps.title: Mamluks and the fall of Acre
steps.text: The Mamluk sultans of Egypt, having stopped the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260, turned on the remaining crusader towns. Baibars took Antioch in 1268, and in 1291 Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil besieged and stormed Acre. The last coastal towns were abandoned within weeks, ending two centuries of crusader states on the mainland, though Cyprus remained in Latin hands.

events.name: Fall of Antioch
events.text: Baibars captured and destroyed the crusader Principality of Antioch.

events.name: Fall of Acre
events.text: The Mamluks stormed the last great crusader city, ending the crusader states.

name: Genpei War
summary: The Minamoto and Taira warrior clans fought a five-year civil war for control of the Japanese court after Taira no Kiyomori placed his infant grandson on the throne. Minamoto no Yoritomo built a power base in the eastern Kanto while his cousin Yoshinaka and brother Yoshitsune drove the Taira from Kyoto and destroyed them at sea at Dan-no-ura in 1185. Yoritomo then founded the Kamakura shogunate, beginning seven centuries of samurai rule.

steps.title: Uji, Ishibashiyama and Fujigawa
steps.text: Prince Mochihito called on the Minamoto to rise against Taira no Kiyomori, but he and his ally Minamoto no Yorimasa were killed after the battle at the Uji bridge near Kyoto. In the east Minamoto no Yoritomo raised his banner in Izu, lost at Ishibashiyama, fled by sea and rebuilt his army in the Kanto with Kamakura as his base. A Taira army under Taira no Koremori marched east but fled at night from the Fuji river, reportedly startled by a flock of waterbirds.

events.name: Battle of Uji
events.text: The Taira crushed the first rising and killed Prince Mochihito.

events.name: Battle of Ishibashiyama
events.text: Yoritomo's small force was routed and he escaped by sea to Awa.

events.name: Battle of Fujigawa
events.text: The Taira army withdrew without fighting, leaving the east to Yoritomo.

steps.label: 1181 to 1183
steps.title: Kurikara and the Taira flight
steps.text: Kiyomori died in 1181 and famine stalled the war. In 1183 Yoritomo's cousin Minamoto no Yoshinaka routed a huge Taira army in a night attack at the Kurikara pass, reportedly driving cattle with torches on their horns into the Taira camp. The Taira abandoned Kyoto, taking the child emperor Antoku and the imperial regalia west, and Yoshinaka entered the capital.

fronts.label: Taira line west of Kyoto, late 1183

events.name: Battle of Kurikara
events.text: Yoshinaka destroyed the main Taira army in the mountains of Etchu.

events.name: Taira abandon Kyoto
events.text: The Taira fled the capital with the child emperor and the regalia.

steps.title: Awazu and Ichi-no-Tani
steps.text: Yoshinaka's troops plundered Kyoto and he quarrelled with the court, so Yoritomo sent his brothers Noriyori and Yoshitsune west, and they killed Yoshinaka at Awazu. The Taira had fortified Ichi-no-Tani on the coast near modern Kobe. While Noriyori attacked from the east, Yoshitsune led horsemen down a steep slope behind the camp, and the Taira fled by sea to Yashima on Shikoku.

events.name: Battle of Awazu
events.text: Yoritomo's brothers defeated and killed their rival cousin Yoshinaka.

events.name: Battle of Ichi-no-Tani
events.text: Yoshitsune's surprise attack from the hills broke the Taira camp.

steps.title: Yashima and Dan-no-ura
steps.text: Yoshitsune crossed to Shikoku in a storm and drove the Taira from Yashima, while Noriyori marched along the Inland Sea coast to cut them off from Kyushu. The Taira fleet under Taira no Tomomori made its last stand in the Shimonoseki strait. At Dan-no-ura the tide turned against them, many Taira leaders drowned themselves, and the child emperor Antoku died with the sacred sword.

events.name: Battle of Yashima
events.text: Yoshitsune's surprise landing drove the Taira from their island base.

events.name: Battle of Dan-no-ura
events.text: The Taira fleet was destroyed and the clan's leaders died, ending the war.

name: Mongol conquests
summary: Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes in 1206 and launched campaigns that his sons and grandsons carried from Korea and China to Russia, Poland, Hungary and the Middle East. Mobile horse archers, captured siege engineers and deliberate terror built the largest contiguous land empire in history, though Mamluk Egypt, Japan, Dai Viet and Java held them off. The conquests killed millions but also tied East and West together through trade along the Silk Road.

steps.label: 1206 to 1215
steps.title: Genghis Khan turns on China
steps.text: Temujin was proclaimed Genghis Khan in 1206 and forced Western Xia to submit by 1210. In 1211 he invaded the Jurchen Jin empire of northern China, breaking its main army at Yehuling, and in 1215 the Jin capital Zhongdu near modern Beijing fell and was sacked.

events.name: Battle of Yehuling
events.text: The Mongols routed the main Jin field army at the Badger Mouth pass.

events.name: Fall of Zhongdu
events.text: The Jin capital near modern Beijing fell and was sacked after a long blockade.

steps.label: 1219 to 1223
steps.title: Destruction of Khwarazm
steps.text: When the Khwarazm Shah's governor at Otrar massacred a Mongol caravan and its envoys, Genghis Khan marched west with perhaps 100,000 riders. Bukhara, Samarkand, Urgench, Merv and Nishapur fell one after another, Jalal al-Din was beaten on the Indus, and Jebe and Subutai rode round the Caspian to crush the Rus and Cumans on the Kalka.

moves.label: Main army via Otrar to Bukhara and Samarkand
Pursuit of Jalal al-Din to the Indus

events.name: Fall of Samarkand
events.text: The great Khwarazmian city surrendered after a short siege and was plundered.

events.name: Battle of the Indus
events.text: Genghis Khan destroyed Jalal al-Din's army, though the prince escaped by swimming the river.

events.name: Battle of the Kalka River
events.text: Jebe and Subutai crushed an army of Rus princes and Cumans in their first clash with Europe.

steps.label: 1227 to 1234
steps.title: Fall of Xia and Jin
steps.text: Western Xia was annihilated in 1227, the year Genghis Khan died during the campaign. His son and successor Ogedei renewed the war on the Jin while Tolui swung through Song territory to take the Jin from behind, and in 1234 the last Jin emperor died at Caizhou, besieged by Mongols and their Song allies.

moves.label: Main army across the Yellow River

events.name: Fall of Western Xia
events.text: The Xia capital surrendered and its people were massacred as Genghis Khan lay dying.

events.name: Battle of Sanfengshan
events.text: Tolui destroyed the last great Jin field army in a snowstorm.

events.name: Siege of Caizhou
events.text: Mongols and Song allies took the last Jin refuge, ending the dynasty.

steps.label: 1237 to 1242
steps.title: Rus, Poland and Hungary
steps.text: Batu and Subutai led the western campaign, conquering the Volga Bulgars and destroying the principalities of Rus, sacking Ryazan, Vladimir and Kiev. In 1241 one column smashed the Poles and Silesians at Legnica while the main army annihilated the Hungarians at Mohi, but news of Ogedei's death in 1242 drew the Mongols back to the steppe.

events.name: Siege of Kiev
events.text: The Mongols stormed and devastated the old capital of Rus.

events.name: Battle of Legnica
events.text: A Mongol column destroyed the army of Duke Henry II of Silesia.

events.name: Battle of Mohi
events.text: Batu and Subutai annihilated the army of King Bela IV of Hungary.

steps.label: 1256 to 1260
steps.title: Baghdad and Ain Jalut
steps.text: Great Khan Mongke sent his brother Hulagu west. He destroyed the Assassin castles of Alamut and in 1258 sacked Baghdad, killing the last Abbasid caliph, then took Aleppo and Damascus. When Hulagu withdrew most of his army, the Mamluks of Egypt under Qutuz and Baibars destroyed the force left under Kitbuqa at Ain Jalut, and the Euphrates became the frontier.

events.name: Siege of Baghdad
events.text: Hulagu sacked the Abbasid capital and ended five centuries of the caliphate there.

events.name: Battle of Ain Jalut
events.text: The Mamluks dealt the Mongols their first great defeat and saved Egypt.

steps.label: 1268 to 1279
steps.title: Kublai conquers the Song
steps.text: Kublai Khan, who founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271, besieged the twin river fortresses of Xiangyang and Fancheng for five years until Persian counterweight trebuchets broke them. Bayan then drove down the Yangtze to take the Song capital Lin'an in 1276, and the last Song loyalists were destroyed at sea off Yamen in 1279.

events.name: Siege of Xiangyang
events.text: The fall of the key Song fortress opened the Yangtze to the Mongols.

events.name: Fall of Lin'an
events.text: The Song court surrendered its capital to Bayan without a fight.

events.name: Battle of Yamen
events.text: The Yuan fleet destroyed the last Song court and fleet, ending the dynasty.

steps.label: 1274 and 1281
steps.title: The invasions of Japan
steps.text: By now the empire had split into four khanates, but Kublai still sought new conquests. His Mongol, Chinese and Korean fleets landed at Hakata Bay in 1274 and again in 1281, when the Japanese had built a stone wall along the shore; both times the samurai held the beaches and typhoons, the kamikaze or divine wind, wrecked the fleets.

events.name: First invasion, Hakata Bay
events.text: The invaders won ashore but re-embarked and lost many ships to a storm.

events.name: Second invasion and the kamikaze
events.text: A typhoon destroyed the huge combined fleet sheltering off Takashima.

steps.label: 1277 to 1294
steps.title: The limits of conquest
steps.text: In Southeast Asia the Yuan broke the kingdom of Pagan in Burma, but Dai Viet under Tran Hung Dao defeated three invasions, the last on the stakes of the Bach Dang river in 1288. A fleet sent to punish Java in 1293 was turned on and driven out by Raden Wijaya, founder of Majapahit, and when Kublai died in 1294 the age of Mongol expansion was over.

events.name: Fall of Pagan
events.text: The Yuan invasion shattered the Pagan kingdom, which broke into rival states.

events.name: Battle of Bach Dang
events.text: Tran Hung Dao trapped the Yuan fleet on iron-tipped stakes planted in the river.

events.name: Mongol expedition to Java
events.text: Raden Wijaya used the Mongols to defeat Kediri, then attacked and drove them out.

name: Albigensian Crusade
summary: Pope Innocent III called a crusade against the Cathar heretics of Languedoc and the southern lords who tolerated them, chief among them Count Raymond VI of Toulouse. Northern French barons under Simon de Montfort conquered much of the south, lost it again after his death, and the French crown finished the job under Louis VIII. The Treaty of Paris in 1229 brought Languedoc under the kings of France and the Inquisition then rooted out the Cathars.

steps.label: 1208 to 1209
steps.title: Béziers and Carcassonne
steps.text: After a papal legate was murdered in 1208, Innocent III proclaimed a crusade, and a large northern army gathered at Lyon and marched down the Rhône. In July 1209 it stormed Béziers and massacred its people, Catholics and Cathars alike. Carcassonne surrendered weeks later, its lord Raymond-Roger Trencavel died in captivity, and his lands were given to Simon de Montfort.

events.name: Massacre at Béziers
events.text: The crusaders stormed Béziers and killed much of its population.

events.name: Surrender of Carcassonne
events.text: Trencavel's capital fell after a short siege, and Simon de Montfort took his lands.

steps.label: 1210 to 1213
steps.title: Montfort's conquests and Muret
steps.text: Simon de Montfort took the Cathar strongholds of Minerve and Lavaur, burning hundreds of heretics, but failed to take Toulouse in 1211. King Peter II of Aragon, overlord of many southern lords, crossed the Pyrenees to protect his vassals and joined Raymond VI. At Muret in September 1213 Montfort's much smaller force charged and killed Peter, and the southern army collapsed.

events.name: Siege of Lavaur
events.text: Montfort took Lavaur and burned some 400 Cathars.

events.name: Battle of Muret
events.text: Peter II was killed and the Aragonese-Occitan army routed.

steps.label: 1215 to 1218
steps.title: The siege of Toulouse
steps.text: The Fourth Lateran Council in 1215 gave Toulouse to Simon de Montfort and stripped Raymond VI of his lands. Raymond's son, the young Raymond VII, retook Beaucaire on the Rhône in 1216, and in 1217 Raymond VI slipped back into Toulouse, which rose for him. Montfort besieged the city, and in June 1218 a stone from a mangonel worked by the townswomen killed him.

events.name: Siege of Beaucaire
events.text: Raymond VII took Beaucaire, the first great southern victory.

events.name: Siege of Toulouse
events.text: Simon de Montfort was killed by a stone and the siege was abandoned.

steps.label: 1219 to 1224
steps.title: The southern recovery
steps.text: Simon's son Amaury de Montfort lacked his father's skill and money, and the southern lords won back town after town. In January 1224 Amaury abandoned Carcassonne and returned north. He handed his rights in the south to King Louis VIII, turning a baronial crusade into a royal conquest.

events.name: Amaury leaves Carcassonne
events.text: The Trencavel heir returned to Carcassonne as the crusaders withdrew.

steps.label: 1226 to 1229
steps.title: The royal crusade and the Treaty of Paris
steps.text: Louis VIII led a royal army down the Rhône in 1226 and took Avignon after a three-month siege, and most southern towns submitted. The king died on the way home, but his commander Humbert de Beaujeu kept up a war of devastation around Toulouse. Exhausted, Raymond VII accepted the Treaty of Paris in 1229, giving up much of his land and marrying his heiress to a French prince, which brought Languedoc to the crown.

events.name: Siege of Avignon
events.text: Avignon fell to Louis VIII and the south largely submitted.

events.name: Treaty of Paris
events.text: Raymond VII submitted, and Languedoc passed to the French crown.

name: Edward I's conquest of Wales
summary: Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, Prince of Wales, ruled most of Wales from his mountain heartland of Gwynedd until he refused homage to Edward I of England. Two English invasions, in 1277 and 1282 to 1283, used sea power and slow coastal advances to strangle Gwynedd, and Llywelyn's death at Orewin Bridge ended independent Welsh rule. Edward secured the conquest with the Statute of Rhuddlan and a ring of great stone castles.

steps.title: The first war
steps.text: Llywelyn refused to do homage, and Edward attacked from three directions: Mortimer from the Marches, Payn de Chaworth in the south, and the king himself along the north coast from Chester, building roads and forts as he went. His fleet seized Anglesey and its harvest, the breadbasket of Gwynedd, and the starving Welsh accepted the Treaty of Aberconwy, which confined Llywelyn to Gwynedd west of the Conwy.

moves.label: Royal army along the north coast

events.name: Treaty of Aberconwy
events.text: Llywelyn kept his title but lost everything east of the Conwy and paid heavy fines.

steps.title: Revolt and the death of Llywelyn
steps.text: On Palm Sunday 1282 Llywelyn's brother Dafydd stormed Hawarden castle, and all of Wales rose. Edward advanced again along the coast, but Luke de Tany's force crossing a bridge of boats from Anglesey was destroyed at Moel-y-Don. Llywelyn then went south to raise mid Wales, and on 11 December he was killed near Builth at Orewin Bridge.

moves.label: Royal army to Rhuddlan and the Conwy
Bridge of boats over the Menai

events.name: Attack on Hawarden
events.text: Dafydd's surprise attack on the English castle began the final war.

events.name: Battle of Moel-y-Don
events.text: The Welsh routed an English force crossing the Menai Strait.

events.name: Battle of Orewin Bridge
events.text: Llywelyn, the last native Prince of Wales, was killed and his army broken.

steps.label: 1283 to 1284
steps.title: Gwynedd falls
steps.text: Edward kept campaigning through the winter. His armies took Dolwyddelan, the Earl of Pembroke captured Castell y Bere, and Dafydd was hunted down in the mountains in June 1283 and executed at Shrewsbury. The Statute of Rhuddlan in 1284 annexed the principality to the English crown, guarded by new castles at Conwy, Caernarfon and Harlech.

moves.label: From Aberystwyth to Castell y Bere

events.name: Siege of Castell y Bere
events.text: The last major Welsh castle surrendered in April 1283.

events.name: Capture of Dafydd
events.text: Betrayed and captured near Bera Mawr, Dafydd was executed for treason.

events.name: Statute of Rhuddlan
events.text: Wales was annexed and divided into English-style shires.

name: Hundred Years' War
summary: The English Plantagenet kings fought the French Valois kings for over a century over English lands in France and Edward III's claim to the French crown. England won famous victories at Crecy, Poitiers and Agincourt and under Henry V held northern France, but Joan of Arc and a reformed French army with powerful artillery drove the English out of everything except Calais. The war forged national identities in both countries and helped end the age of the armoured knight.

steps.label: 1337 to 1340
steps.title: War at sea
steps.text: Philip VI confiscated Edward III's duchy of Aquitaine in 1337, and Edward answered by claiming the French crown through his mother. The first great clash came at sea: in 1340 the English fleet caught the French navy packed in the harbour of Sluys and destroyed it, winning control of the Channel for the invasions to come.

events.name: Battle of Sluys
